A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same local Fisher score matching work. Their text, equations, figures and complete appendices are readable, and corresponding material can be matched despite restructuring and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian simulation experiments, confidence-interval coverage and runtime analyses, LSST weak-lensing experiments, and MNIST generator-inversion results in Section 7 and Appendices A.9–A.11.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds curvature sensitivity, higher-dimensional estimation and neural-network FSM comparisons in Section 5.2 and Appendices A.11–A.13.

M1.justification: v2 Appendix A.4 adds a neural-network score-model variant trained by backpropagation at each parameter iterate. This extends the parameterization while retaining the FSM objective, default linear estimator and outer optimization algorithm. Proposal grid-search tuning was already described in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions cover Gaussian and shifted-exponential examples, LSST-Y10 weak-lensing simulations, and GAN inversion using 16×16 MNIST. The added dimensionality, curvature and score-model comparisons vary configurations within these retained tasks.

E2.justification: Neural-network FSM becomes an evaluated comparator to linear FSM in Gaussian estimation, interval coverage, weak lensing and generator inversion (v2 Figures 10–11 and 14–16). KDE-SP, NLE, direct optimization and bootstrap comparisons remain. The Bertl citation update does not introduce a different baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds a fixed-budget, 1,000-simulation parameter-accuracy sweep over dimensions 2–100, extends the existing budget sweeps from dimensions 5 and 20 to include 50 and 100, and adds 20-dimensional gradient sensitivity. Figure 2 introduces two likelihood-curvature settings evaluated using MSE and estimator standard deviation. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v2 systematically tests linear versus neural score parameterization, including its effect on confidence-interval calibration. It adds curvature-dependent proposal-scale sensitivity and broader dimensional robustness analyses. Appendix A.5 also reports that attempted proposal annealing produced no meaningful gains, although this comparison lacks detailed quantitative results.

E5.justification: v1 already reports repeated runs and 95% confidence intervals for gradient comparisons. v2's checklist adds a broader statement identifying experimental error bars as 95% intervals over 100 runs. This expands reporting rather than establishing additional runs or a new statistical procedure; timing captions still specify 1,000 runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for higher dimensions and neural FSM, including deteriorating neural performance at high dimensions and declining interval coverage with more observations (Figures 10–11 and 14). Figure 2 adds curvature-dependent proposal-scale optima. Retained results also change: at dimension 5 and 100 simulations, plotted FSM parameter error is approximately 0.25 in v1 Figure 3 versus 0.22 in v2 Figure 11.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 replaces v1's joint-expectation first-order shortcut with a conditional-expectation derivation. v2 also explicitly defines the proposal-marginal denominator in the bias proof and corrects the concavity assumption's dataset log-likelihood to a sum over observations. The principal theorem statements and convergence framework remain.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions and conclusion retain the central claims: efficient likelihood-free MLE through local FSM, a closed-form linear estimator, a Gaussian-smoothing connection and favorable empirical performance. Additional comparisons and future directions do not materially redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds an empirical-Bayes interpretation, explains how likelihood curvature affects proposal-scale selection, and discusses anisotropic curvature, expensive covariance tuning and annealing instability. It suggests optimization or overfitting as possible explanations for neural FSM failures and discusses a semi-amortized extension. These substantially expand mechanisms and practical limitations.

D1.justification: v2 first documents the linear regression intercept and specifies neural architectures, ten inner Adam updates and task-specific learning rates. It also explicitly gives six LSST parameters and 50 GAN latent parameters. These are added disclosures; the PDFs do not establish that the intercept or retained applications' dimensions changed.

R1.justification: Section 6 acknowledges Sui et al. as independent work with a similar estimator and distinguishes this paper's MLE focus. It adds Geffner, Sharrock and Jiang on score-based SBI, while Morris supports the empirical-Bayes interpretation. These are targeted positioning additions alongside bibliographic updates to retained works.

P1.justification: v2 polishes language and notation, moves Algorithm 1 from the appendix into Section 4, adds a proposal-distribution subsection and reorganizes experimental appendices. Discussion becomes Conclusion, and acknowledgments and a NeurIPS checklist are added. The main narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds curvature and higher-dimensional plots and incorporates neural curves or boxplots into multiple existing displays. v1 Figure 3 becomes the expanded appendix Figure 11, while a dimension sweep occupies the main text. The main GAN error display gains a panel, and long appendix equations are reformatted into multiline displays.

improvement.justification: v2 better supports the choice of a lightweight linear score model through direct neural comparisons and sensitivity analyses. The intercept disclosure, clearer conditional-expectation proof and fuller proposal-tuning discussion improve reproducibility and understanding. The neural comparison tests a small network with only ten inner updates, limiting broader conclusions; the gains strengthen the existing study without resolving its principal theoretical limitations.
